articles.author: Sachin Rawat
articles.description:
MIT researcher Sharon Gilad-Gutnick has witnessed many children see for the first time. After having their cataracts surgically removed, the children can see the world but don’t recognize faces well. Even among those who can recognize the faces of their parents or others they know well, most don’t look at the faces of the people they speak with.
“If we told them to look at the face, they could usually manage it,” Gilad-Gutnick told Big Think. “But they were mostly looking at the hands.”
Gilad-Gutnick works with these children as part of Project Prakash, an initiative that provides care to children and adults with congenital blindness in India and investigates the neuroscience of sight restoration. Congenital cataracts are a preventable cause of blindness and are often treatable within two …
articles.title: The brain after blindness: How newly-sighted people build a visual world

articles.author: Jeff  DeGraff
articles.description:
In the middle of the 20th century, the British philosopher Gilbert Ryle coined one of the most influential phrases in modern thought: “the ghost in the machine.” He was challenging Cartesian dualism, the idea that the human mind is an invisible pilot steering the body from somewhere behind the eyes. Ryle called this a category mistake. There was no ghost hidden inside the machinery of the human body. Intelligence did not float above behavior; it emerged from it.
Sixty years later, we face a strange reversal.
Instead of imagining a ghost inside ourselves, we are quietly relocating our agency into the machines we build. We are becoming accountable for decisions we no longer meaningfully author.
The inversion is easy to miss. Ryle argued that there was no separate mind steering the body. Toda…
articles.title: The ghost in the machine has changed sides

articles.author: Sara Seager
articles.description:
Astrophysicist Sara Seager has spent decades expanding how we search for life beyond Earth: not by asking what we would look like out there, but by imagining forms of intelligence that may be utterly unlike our own.
Her work explores “technosignatures” — physical clues of advanced life, from satellite swarms to artificial light. As artificial intelligence accelerates here on Earth, Seager considers whether post-biological life might be what awaits us — and whether it already exists elsewhere in the cosmos. Our biggest challenge, she suggests, may be learning to see past the limits of our own imagination.
This video We’ve been looking for life. Here’s why we should look for intelligence instead is featured on Big Think.
articles.title: We’ve been looking for life. Here’s why we should look for intelligence instead

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
Our Sun gravitationally dominates the Solar System.

Here in our own Solar System, the Sun dominates the spacetime within it in nearly all locations. Whereas the environment close to a planet is locally dominated by that planet’s gravity, and the ensuing curvature it imprints on the surrounding spacetime, the Sun’s gravity dominates the larger Solar System environment. Whereas a spacecraft must achieve speeds of 11 km/s to escape from Earth’s gravity, speeds nearly four times as great must be achieved at the Earth-Sun distance to escape from the Solar System entirely.

Credit: T. Pyle/Caltech/MIT/LIGO Lab



Of over 17,000 payloads launched into space, only six will escape the Solar System’s gravity.

The most remarkable fact about Pioneer 10’s trajectory is that it gained nearly the maxim…
articles.title: Only these six spacecraft will ever escape the Solar System

articles.author: Chris Miller
articles.description:
What if the world’s most critical technology isn’t software, but the tiny pieces of silicon that power it? In an age where chips are everywhere, from smartphones to coffee makers, their manufacturing complexity might surprise you. It’s harder to make a modern semiconductor than a nuclear weapon. 
Making this tech both very inexpensive and very small is incredibly difficult. That’s why there’s just a couple of companies in the world who are capable of it.
This video The tiny transistors remaking our global order is featured on Big Think.
articles.title: The tiny transistors remaking our global order

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
Here in our Universe, there’s a big puzzle at the heart of every black hole. According to Einstein’s General Relativity, for every black hole that exists within the Universe, there are only three properties that go into it that matter in any way:
the black hole’s total mass,
the black hole’s net electric charge,
and the black hole’s intrinsic angular momentum,
and that’s it. It doesn’t matter what type of matter (or antimatter, or dark matter) went into the black hole in order to form it; all that matters is its mass, charge, and angular momentum.
But in addition to a Universe governed by Einstein’s General Relativity, we also live in an inherently quantum Universe. Quantum mechanically, there are all sorts of bizarre phenomena that cannot be avoided, from uncertainty to entanglement. It’s…
articles.title: Ask Ethan: Can quantum entanglement survive a black hole?

articles.author: Sam Kean
articles.description:
We tend to imagine ancient life in broad strokes. But daily existence was built out of small, sensory details. The taste of staple foods, the smell of living spaces, the feel of handmade tools in your hands — those experiences shaped the people of the past. 
Sam Kean examines how recreating those details brings history into sharper focus, rebuilding the foods and practices of the past and what that reveals about human adaptability. 
This video How experimental archaeologists are resurrecting our forgotten past is featured on Big Think.
articles.title: How experimental archaeologists are resurrecting our forgotten past

articles.author: Shai Tubali
articles.description:
Sven Nyholm already sees troubling signs among his students. As a Professor of Ethics of Artificial Intelligence at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich, he’s noticed that many can’t be bothered to engage with demanding texts when an AI summary is just seconds away. “AI is designed to make people not think,” he tells Big Think. “But why study philosophy at university if you don’t want to think — if you don’t want to sharpen your critical abilities — and instead outsource them to a mindless AI program?” In these moments, he admits, both his students’ studies and his own role as a teacher feel less meaningful.
Nyholm has spent years contemplating where all this might be heading. As one of the earliest philosophers to examine how AI intersects with meaning in human life, he looks closely at…
articles.title: The hidden cost of letting AI make your life easier

articles.author: Tom Hardin
articles.description:
[In the] summer of 2008, Sue and I kept up the charade of normal life by hunting for a house. We told ourselves it was optimism. In reality, it was desperation disguised as hope; some fragile belief that this whole FBI informant nightmare had an expiration date.
Sue’s dad, Bob, tipped us off about a new build in Westwood. We drove out one humid afternoon, stepped inside, and immediately saw a future we weren’t sure we deserved: four bedrooms, three and a half baths, wide hall-ways that echoed with the promise of kids’ laughter. A quiet street. Neighbors who waved. A front porch that begged for summer nights and cold drinks. We fell hard for the illusion. And like two people pretending they weren’t standing on a fault line, we made an offer.
The down payment came from our savings and what w…
articles.title: Inside Wall Street’s 2008 meltdown, through the eyes of an FBI informant

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
Here on Earth, the very idea of a laser is relatively novel, having only been invented in 1958. The underlying physics is straightforward:
an electron within a molecule gets excited to a higher-energy state,
the electron de-transitions back to the lower energy state,
where it emits light of a very specific wavelength in the process.
Then, pumped or injected energy re-excites an electron within that very same molecule back into that higher-energy state, over and over. This causes light of precisely that same, monochromatic wavelength to get emitted over and over again. So long as you continue stimulating the same transition, you’ll keep getting light of that exact same frequency over and over again, every time.
But out there in the Universe, this exact phenomenon occurs naturally in a numbe…
articles.title: Record-breaking natural laser discovered 11 billion light-years away

articles.author: Jonny Thomson
articles.description:
European folktales often center around three colors: red, black, and white. Snow White has skin as white as snow, lips as red as blood, and hair as black as ebony. In the Grimms’ “Iron Hans,” a young man rides three horses into three battles — a red horse, a black horse, and a white horse. In the Norse tale “Tatterhood,” a red flower and a white flower grow side by side in the dark earth.
This week, I interviewed the mythologist and storyteller Martin Shaw for Mini Philosophy. Shaw’s new book, Liturgies of the Wild, makes the case that folk stories and myths can help us understand ourselves and life more broadly. And in these colors, we find a map of human maturation.
The colors correspond roughly to three modes of being. Each has a gift and a shadow. Each belongs most naturally to a parti…
articles.title: The 3 colors: What folktales teach about how to grow wise

articles.author: Lee Helland, Carina Mia Wong
articles.description:
A woman stands at the edge of the Amazon Rainforest. Behind her, an explosion of life — thousands of animal species, billions of trees, lush canopy. Ahead, another kind: Humanity. 
People from every corner of the Earth fill the city of Belém, Brazil. It’s a sea of color, music, and emotion as they dance and stomp across asphalt, past highrises in the hot, humid air. A paper snake the length of a city block ripples overhead.
The woman wipes sweat from her temples. Her purple baseball cap is soaked through, its message blunt:
DERECHOS A LA TIERRA ¡YA!
Land rights — now.

Photo by Natalia Ramírez Gutiérrez
The woman is Joan Carling, a human rights activist and the executive director of Indigenous Peoples Rights International (IPRI). The scene unfolded at COP30, the climate summit hosted by th…
articles.title: Widening the frame: Indigenous land rights and the future of climate policy

articles.author: Nilofer Merchant
articles.description:
It’s called the Gladiator Strategy. 
The Swiss CEO of a shoe company stirred his espresso as he tried to convince me of his preferred way of working: “I think a battle of ideas is so important. It helps us fight things out, so the one idea left standing is the absolute best idea.” 
In Roman times, the best gladiators weren’t necessarily the best athletes or the strongest physical performers but the ones who knew how to entertain the crowds in the way the emperor loved. Whatever, whoever amused the emperor was given the thumbs-­up. The workplace parallel is perhaps obvious: People can “win” internal fights in those boardrooms by arguing for the ideas and perspectives that the boss already loves. So “fighting for the best idea” becomes a public way to endorse and validate the emperor’s —­ er…
articles.title: Thumbs-down to “Gladiator Strategy”? Try the Nadella philosophy instead

articles.author: Tim Brinkhof
articles.description:
Sometimes, when Jim Belushi feels anxious, he tells himself he’s actually just stoked. “Physiologically,” the actor, comedian, and entrepreneur tells Big Think, “what happens to your body when you’re nervous or fearful is exactly the same thing as what happens when you’re excited,” so all you need to do is flip a switch. It’s one of several tricks he learned early in life that stuck with him throughout the various chapters of his long and storied career, from Hollywood to Oregon pot farm.
Born to Albanian-American parents in the suburbs of Chicago, Belushi began acting in high school — an experience, he once told the Connecticut Post, that “made me feel good for the first time in my life.” Following in the footsteps of elder sibling John Belushi, he cut his teeth at Chicago’s renowned Seco…
articles.title: How to conquer pressure — the Jim Belushi way

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
Here on Earth, it seems easy and straight forward to know “where” anything is, or to know “when” an event either occurred or will occur. After all, we’ve mapped out the entire surface of the Earth, and can define our location with three coordinates — latitude, longitude, and altitude/depth — no matter where in the world we are. Additionally, we’ve synchronized all methods of timekeeping here on Earth with atomic clocks, enabling people from all different locations on Earth to know both the “when” and “where” any event occurs, will occur, or has occurred.
But this relies on an underlying assumption that most of us make without ever thinking twice about it: that you, from your location on Earth, are observing the same “here and now” as anyone else in any other location on Earth. Unfortunatel…
articles.title: How Einstein revolutionized the meaning of “where” and “when”

articles.author: Hannah Ritchie
articles.description:
I read Mark Lynas’s book Six Degrees: Our Future on a Hotter Planet when I was 14 years old, and it scared the life out of me. Lynas takes the reader on a journey of what to expect from a world that’s one degree warmer, two degrees, three degrees, all the way up to six degrees. By the middle of the book, your blood pressure is high; by the end, you’re on the floor.
It is a well-researched book that offers us a window into many possible futures. Fortunately, the scientific consensus has moved away from the most extreme scenarios since its publication. Unfortunately, a lot of the public messaging has not. Many people believe a pathway to 5°C or 6°C is already locked in, and the only thing we can do now is prepare for the worst.
Let’s look at what the latest science says about where we might …
articles.title: Don’t let climate fatalism become a self-fulfilling prophecy

articles.author: Adam Dietz
articles.description:
On a rough day, it’s rarely the workload that breaks you. It’s the human layer: the meeting that turns tense, the work chat message you read as disrespect, the impulse to fire off a reply that feels righteous for thirty seconds and costly for a week. In those moments, emotional intelligence is basically the difference between staying aligned and creating unforced errors.
You may not control the situation, but you can control how you meet it. You can stay aligned, or drift into unforced errors: reactive words, sloppy decisions, needless conflict.
Confucius even gives a compact checklist for this: nine “states of mind” to return to in the middle of ordinary life. In the Analects he writes:
The superior person has nine states of mind:
for eyes: bright
for ears: penetrating
for countenance: co…
articles.title: 9 Confucian rules for emotional intelligence at work

articles.author: Alain de Botton
articles.description:
For most of human history, love was not a choice we made, love was a choice made for us. By our family, our class, or by means of survival. 
Now that love has been liberated, it seems to have become more complicated and more illusive than ever. Alain de Botton explains.
This video Why relationships in 2026 carry impossible expectations is featured on Big Think.
articles.title: Why relationships in 2026 carry impossible expectations

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
However you feel about artificial intelligence (AI) — and, in particular, about the large language models and chatbots that are powered by it — the reality is that humanity is currently building and expanding infrastructure to support it. This includes large networks of power-demanding and water-requiring data centers that are being constructed, often conflicting with the electricity and water needs of the humans who live in those locations. It’s because of these concerns that some have floated the idea of AI data centers in space, with one company, SpaceX, recently announcing plans to build a literal megaconstellation of one million satellites to further that ambition.
Is this an example of an emerging technology that could provide an off-world solution to the problem of competing demands…
articles.title: The 5 biggest obstacles to AI data centers in space

articles.author: Kate Bowler
articles.description:
Toxic positivity has become a cultural system in America, says historian and professor Kate Bowler.
She traces how optimism became an emotional mandate in American life: a belief that bright sides and silver linings can solve anything. But when positivity refuses pain, it stops being hopeful and becomes denial.
Drawing on personal experience and cultural analysis, Bowler reveals how forced optimism erases nuance, stigmatizes grief, and leaves us unprepared for the parts of life that don’t resolve. Some things aren’t meant to be mastered — they just hurt. Naming that, she argues, is the first step toward something more honest, and more human.
This video Why toxic positivity is making us miserable is featured on Big Think.
articles.title: Why toxic positivity is making us miserable

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
What, exactly, composes the Universe?

In order for life to emerge within the Universe, the chemical precursor ingredients need to be delivered to an environment where life can arise, sustain itself, and thrive. This cannot happen until the elements required for life, including carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and phosphorus, exist. None of them were created in the hot Big Bang; only later on in the interiors of their stars and through physical processes arising from their life and death cycles.

Credit: NASA Goddard/CI Lab/Dan Gallagher


In antiquity, many opined about “the elements” in combination.

It used to be thought, more than 2500 years ago, that there were fundamental “elements” to the Universe that combined to make everything up. These elements varied from culture to culture and philos…
articles.title: How our view of “fundamental” has evolved over time

articles.author: Kevin Dickinson
articles.description:
An unfortunate side effect of reading philosopher C. Thi Nguyen’s latest book, The Score, is noticing how much sway metrics hold over you. I say “unfortunate” not because the realization is unwelcome, quite the opposite, but because you’ll find yourself taking account of the numerical scrum in your life. And that exercise gets unnerving fast.
KPIs, BMIs, OKRs, credit scores, savings rates, social media likes, screen time, steps walked, hours worked, hours slept, to-dos done, to-dos still to do, books read, practice hours, blood pressure readings, calories consumed, macronutrient ratios, the list just keeps going. Heck, even those stressed-out smiley faces on your meditation app mask yet one more metric. Some of these are forced on us by our employers or our societies; others we willfully a…
articles.title: Your life, scored: How metrics warp your sense of meaning

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
If we’re willing to think about the future, the farther ahead we extrapolate, the farther along the inevitable path towards our thermodynamic end state: the heat death of the Universe. Star-formation will eventually end, and then the last shining stars will burn out. Galaxies will dissociate due to gravitational interactions, ejecting all masses and leaving only supermassive black holes behind. And then those black holes will decay via Hawking radiation, leaving only cold, stable, isolated bodies, from which no further energy can be extracted, all accelerating away from us within our dark energy-dominated Universe.
At least, that’s what will happen in our far future based on our current cosmic picture: the best one we’ve figured out as of 2026. But this troubles a great many people, includ…
articles.title: Ask Ethan: Will anything persist when the Universe dies?

articles.author: Alain de Botton
articles.description:
We want to believe that love is guided by instinct, and that following our heart will lead us to our ideal soulmate. Alain de Botton argues that our romantic lives are shaped more by the emotional patterns we learned in childhood than by destiny.
This video Why healthy love feels uncomfortable to so many people is featured on Big Think.
articles.title: Why healthy love feels uncomfortable to so many people

articles.author: Ross Pomeroy
articles.description:
In Andy Weir’s bestselling novel The Martian, foul-mouthed protagonist Mark Watney “sciences the shit” out of his circumstances to survive being stranded on Mars. The result is an engrossing work of science fiction, particularly captivating for its apparent realism. Watney ekes out an existence by eating potatoes sowed in Martian soil fertilized by his own feces. He shelters from the frigid conditions in his above-ground habitation unit, huddling around a repurposed, radiating nuclear battery. 
Watney’s survivalist experience isn’t exactly an advertisement from the Red Planet’s tourist board, but it does romanticize space settlement, showcasing humanity’s ability to heroically persist beyond our “blue marble.” Readers are left with the sense that living on Mars is not just possible, but pr…
articles.title: Science fiction blinded us to the perils of settling Mars

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
The idea of the Big Bang has captivated the imagination of humanity since it was first proposed nearly a full 100 years ago. Since the Universe is expanding today (as observations have indicated since the 1920s), then we can extrapolate back, earlier and earlier, to when it was smaller, younger, denser, and hotter. You could go back as far as you can imagine: before humans, before the stars, before there were even neutral atoms. At the earliest times of all, you’d make all the particles and antiparticles possible, including the fundamental ones that we cannot create at our low energies today.
As time went forward, the Universe would cool, expand, and gravitate all together. First atomic nuclei would form from protons and neutrons, then neutral atoms would form, and then gravitation would l…
articles.title: The Big Bang’s final and most difficult prediction: confirmed

articles.author: Big Think
articles.description: In this monthly issue, we explore the bleeding edge of biotech, as well as the scientists, writers, and philosophers whose efforts helped get us here.
articles.title: Biology’s New Era

articles.author: Adam Frank
articles.description:
We are living in the age of maximum AI hype: A superintelligence that surpasses humanity is going to emerge at any moment, according to the most breathless corners of the tech world.
There are basic technical grounds to be skeptical of that claim, but beyond that, a much deeper issue lies at the boundary between science and philosophy: What makes life different from non-life? Why is a rock inert and insensate, while even the simplest cell manifests open-ended activity in the relentless pursuit of staying alive? Since the only systems that indisputably display intelligence are alive, if we can’t understand life, we’re probably missing something essential about intelligence. 
Sixty years ago, an influential but little-known philosopher named Hans Jonas gave a potent, creative, and radical an…
articles.title: Why organisms are more than machines

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
Planet Earth is overrun with life. Lakes, rivers, seas, and oceans are teeming with it, from the surfaces all the way down to the bottom, often at depths of miles and miles. The land, both above and below ground, is packed with living organisms of varying size, mass, and complexity, including plants, animals, and fungi. Even the atmosphere houses a wide variety of life forms, from birds and insects to microbes found far above the highest mountain peaks. All told, more than 8 million species of organisms are currently represented on Earth, totaling over half a trillion tonnes of carbon in overall biomass.
We can trace our evolutionary history through time, with notable milestones including:
the development of mammals and plants,
the emergence of sexual reproduction and multicellularity,
the…
articles.title: Metabolism, not cells or genetics, may have begun life on Earth

articles.author: Kristin Houser
articles.description:
Long before biologists could edit genes, grow embryos in the lab, or connect computers to the human brain, science-fiction writers were already imagining these biotechnologies and how they might reshape society — for better or (usually) for worse.
But sci-fi writers aren’t psychics. While the five novels below did foreshadow modern biotech, their authors’ visions of the tools leading us toward dystopia — or dinosaurs run amok — haven’t materialized. Instead, these technologies are helping people treat diseases, regain lost abilities, and build the families of their dreams.
That all may not be as pulse-pounding as a Velociraptor attack, but it’s every bit as world-changing.
Brave New World by Aldous Huxley (1932)
Foreshadowed: In vitro fertilization 


English author Aldous Huxley’s dystopi…
articles.title: 5 sci-fi books that foreshadowed the future of biology

articles.author: Jen Kirby
articles.description:
The barriers to reading, writing, and editing DNA are falling fast. A scientist can now order synthetic gene sequences from manufacturers and have them within days — soon, it could be common to produce them right in the lab using a benchtop DNA synthesizer. High school students are learning CRISPR gene-editing techniques. Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms trained on biological data are accelerating experimentation and generating sequences that don’t exist in nature. 
The hope is that these developments will lead to new breakthroughs in healthcare, agriculture, energy, and more. The fear is that they will lower the threshold for profound misuse of biotech, while simultaneously increasing the scale of what bad actors can accomplish. The risks aren’t hypothetical — in early February, the…
articles.title: How to deter biothreats in the age of gene synthesis

articles.author: Alex Hutchinson
articles.description:
When horse racing fans rhapsodize about Secretariat’s enormous heart, they’re not speaking metaphorically — a postmortem exam in 1989 found that it weighed between 21 and 22 pounds, two-and-a-half times more than the average thoroughbred’s heart. The legendary horse also had a perfectly proportioned bone structure, flawless biomechanics, and a seemingly innate hunger for the finish line. 
In 1973, he not only swept the Triple Crown — the Kentucky Derby, the Preakness Stakes, and the Belmont Stakes — but also set records in all three races, winning the Belmont by 31 lengths. Those records still stand more than half a century later, and with each passing year, it seems increasingly clear that Secretariat was as good as horses get.
Whether humans, too, have reached peak performance is a quest…
articles.title: Athletes keep breaking records — and they may never stop

articles.author: Anne-Laure Le Cunff
articles.description:
There’s a feeling I love almost more than anything: the feeling of sinking into a good book while the world around me fades away. My breathing slows, my shoulders drop, and the mental chatter in the back of my mind goes quiet.
What’s happening in those moments goes far deeper than entertainment or education, and we seem to sense this instinctively. Reading is relaxing, and many people do it as a counterbalance to our overstimulated age.
But what exactly is happening when we read? What’s going on beneath the surface that makes reading a book feel so restorative?
The answer lies in how reading changes our neurochemistry in real time. Reading isn’t just about decoding words on a page. It’s a complex neurochemical process that affects everything from our heart rate to our hormone levels.
The n…
articles.title: How reading books regulates your nervous system

articles.author: Peter Leyden
articles.description:
The start of the Bioengineering Age is a very big deal for everyone on Earth, and not just because of its potential to improve human health. In the long run, the arrival of advanced bioengineering technologies will help make this planet truly sustainable, too.
The world of biology is going through a transformation that is every bit as profound as the ones kicking off the AI Age and the Clean Energy Age. In fact, what is going on in this field is very similar to what is going on in those other two fields: They each have crossed an engineering threshold.
The arrival of AI has turned intelligence into a technology. For all of human history, intelligence has been housed in complex, mushy brains that we still don’t really understand — let alone know how to engineer. Now we have machines that ar…
articles.title: How bioengineering will help save the planet

articles.author: Adam Frank
articles.description:
We are living in the age of maximum AI hype: A superintelligence that surpasses humanity is going to emerge at any moment, according to the most breathless corners of the tech world.
There are basic technical grounds to be skeptical of that claim, but beyond that, a much deeper issue lies at the boundary between science and philosophy: What makes life different from non-life? Why is a rock inert and insensate, while even the simplest cell manifests open-ended activity in the relentless pursuit of staying alive? Since the only systems that indisputably display intelligence are alive, if we can’t understand life, we’re probably missing something essential about intelligence. 
Sixty years ago, an influential but little-known philosopher named Hans Jonas gave a potent, creative, and radical an…
articles.title: Why organisms are more than machines

articles.author: Thomas Moynihan
articles.description:
After eluding his Japanese captors, an escaped prisoner of war found himself stranded on a previously unknown archipelago in the South Pacific in 1941. There, the Allied soldier discovered a species of mammal that walked on its nose. The creatures were later named rhinogrades, or, more colloquially, “snouters.”
An idiosyncratic order of mammals comprising 138 species descended from a shrew-like ancestor, Rhinogradentia are typified by their luxuriant, exuberant noses. Some locomote by hopping, using their nasal appendage like a muscular flipper; others are sessile, attracting insects with flower-like petals that blossom from their nostril cartilage. Most rhinogrades have one nose, but some have evolved multiple proboscises, which they use for walking and hunting, like furry terrestrial oct…
articles.title: Snouters, dinosauroids, and other animals that never were

articles.author: Dirk Schulze-Makuch, Tony Reichhardt
articles.description:
The diversity of life on our planet is amazing, especially considering it all begins with essentially the same ingredients — every cellular organism that has ever existed, from bacteria and birch trees to dinosaurs and humans, is built on DNA-based biochemistry.
But how much more diverse might life be on other worlds? Planets with different geology and chemistry, orbiting different types of stars, could yield an endless variety of life-forms.
Science fiction authors and filmmakers have already imagined some of the possibilities. Here, we look at five sci-fi aliens to see how they measure up against modern scientific thinking about what kinds of extraterrestrial life might exist.
1. Mr. Spock: The humanoids

Paramount Pictures Corp.
Filmmakers often give us human-looking aliens, presumably …
articles.title: 5 sci-fi aliens — and the likelihood they could actually exist

articles.author: Frank Jacobs
articles.description:
In an abandoned cemetery on Cuba’s Isla de la Juventud stands the weathered headstone of Estefania Koenig. When she died in 1981, at the ripe old age of 95, she was the last American of what had once been called the McKinley Colonies. A century ago, it was a thriving citrus-growing community, American in everything except the letter of the law. Then came a couple of devastating hurricanes — and the closure of a geopolitical loophole.
A forgotten footnote in American history
The story of the McKinley Colonies is more than a forgotten footnote in history. William McKinley, the 25th president of the United States (from 1897 until his assassination in 1901), was America’s last unabashed expansionist-in-chief. Under his watch, the U.S. snapped up Guam, the Philippines, Puerto Rico, and Cuba fro…
articles.title: Welcome to McKinley: How the U.S. almost colonized a chunk of Cuba

articles.author: Angus Fletcher
articles.description:
Trillions of dollars are now at risk because global investors are making the same mistake that caused the dot-com bubble, Black Friday, and the 1929 Wall Street crash. The mistake is: To believe that numbers can predict the future.
The mistake originates in logic. Logic reduces life to statistics. And statistics convert real-world business into spreadsheets of digits: total income, net profit, employee productivity. . . Those mathematical values are then scoured by logic for patterns and trends. Which is to say: The spreadsheets are fed into AI machine learning systems or analyzed by traders who (by engaging Daniel Kahneman’s system 2) have rigorously purged their minds of bias. Until — with probabilistic precision — the cost of future commodities is computed, prompting a set of rational e…
articles.title: Why Warren Buffett’s superpower is an Achilles heel for AI

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
In all the known Universe, at least as of 2026, the only world known to support life is planet Earth. Despite all we’ve learned about the Universe, including:
the vast abundance of exoplanets,
including rocky exoplanets with Earth-like temperatures,
the ubiquity of heavy elements,
the commonness of organic molecules that are known precursors to life,
and the long cosmic timescales over which stars with such planets form,
there are no known examples of worlds, other than our own, where life processes or definitive biosignatures have been detected.
Although we’ve just recently discovered our 6000th confirmed exoplanet, we’ve sent spacecraft — including orbiters, landers, and even rovers — to a wide variety of planets and moons in our own Solar System, and we’ve been listening for signs of ex…
articles.title: The biggest overlooked problem in the hunt for alien Earths

articles.author: Richard E. Cytowic
articles.description:
Your brain isn’t broken, but it may seem like that because of how the screen age overwhelms your biology. 
Neurologist Richard Cytowic argues that attention is a finite energy budget, not a virtue, and modern life is engineered to exhaust it.
This video The biological necessity of boredom in the age of screens is featured on Big Think.
articles.title: The biological necessity of boredom in the age of screens

articles.author: Sara Seager
articles.description:
Sara Seager, a planetary scientist, astrophysicist, and leading researcher in the search for life beyond Earth, examines how discovering life elsewhere would represent a Copernican-level shift in human understanding. 
Research into Mars, Venus, and the icy moons of Jupiter and Saturn has revealed complex molecules and liquid environments that could support life. Independent origins of life would imply that the galaxy is rich with living individuals, challenging long-held cultural, religious, and philosophical assumptions. The acceptance of major scientific discoveries — and the unexpected practical contributions to pure science — impact how the search for extraterrestrial life may benefit society over time.
This video We may find alien life, but will we be able to accept the consequences? is featured on Big Think.
articles.title: We may find alien life, but will we be able to accept the consequences?

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
In terms of making things happen, energy is an indispensable consideration.

When we see something like a ball balanced precariously atop a hill, this appears to be what we call a finely-tuned state, or a state of unstable equilibrium. A much more stable position is for the ball to be down somewhere at the bottom of the valley. What we currently conceive of as our Universe’s zero-point energy may not actually be the lowest-energy state possible, which means that a transition, and an accompanying energy extraction event, may be possible.

Credit: L. Albarez-Gaume & J. Ellis, Nature Physics, 2011


Systems spontaneously tend towards the lowest-energy state.

In many physical instances, you can find yourself trapped in a local, false minimum, unable to reach the lowest-energy state, which is …
articles.title: What are the most energy-efficient reactions in physics?

articles.author: Tim Brinkhof
articles.description:
Americans are getting worse at math. Student scores have fallen to their lowest point in decades. Nearly half of high school students barely meet what the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP) considers a “basic” level of comprehension, and more than 900 freshmen at the University of California, San Diego — 12.5% of the institution’s first-year class in 2024 — had the mathematical proficiency of a 13-year-old.
U.S. adults aren’t faring much better. Last checked, only 65% could pass a basic arithmetic test, making the country one of the more quantitatively challenged in the industrialized world.
But this isn’t the first time the math graph has trended downward. A similar development took place during the early stages of the Cold War, when enrollment in high school algebra fell …
articles.title: It’s never too late to stop hating math

articles.author: Scott Solomon
articles.description:
Outer space is having a moment. NASA’s Artemis 2 mission is about to take humans farther into space than we have ever gone; SpaceX is preparing to test the latest version of Starship, its interplanetary transport system; and just today, a crew of four astronauts flew to the International Space Station to replace the team that was evacuated last month due to a medical emergency. These efforts are part of a common vision: expanding humanity’s presence beyond Earth, including the eventual creation of human settlements on Mars.
But what would it be like to live on Mars? Aside from the challenges of lower gravity, intense radiation, and toxic soil, an important, but less often considered, factor would be your love life.
People have been traveling to space for more than six decades and have been…
articles.title: Love in low gravity: The surprisingly high stakes of sex in space

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description:
One of the most mind-bending concepts about the Universe is the idea that the very fabric of space itself is expanding. It was proven, way back in 1922, that this is an inevitable consequence of having a Universe that’s filled, in a near-uniform fashion, with any type (or types) of energy at all. Such a Universe cannot be static and stable, but must, in the context of General Relativity, either expand or contract. When this theoretical framework was combined with observational data measuring the distance to, and redshift of, galaxies external to our own Milky Way, the fact of the expanding Universe was established observationally.
It’s now a full century later, and we’ve learned — to a great degree of accuracy — how quickly the Universe itself is expanding, as well as what forms of energy …
articles.title: Ask Ethan: Can we see the expanding Universe changing?

articles.author: Chris Miller
articles.description:
The story of the chip is a story about geopolitics and scarcity. From $20 billion fabrication plants to machines built by a single Dutch firm, the supply chain behind your devices is both miraculous and astonishingly fragile. 
Chris Miller explains why the AI race, U.S.–China tensions, and the future of economic dominance, all rest on this tiny square of silicon. 
This video The most important piece of technology in your lifetime is this tiny chip is featured on Big Think.
articles.title: The most important piece of technology in your lifetime is this tiny chip

articles.author: Tom Griffiths
articles.description:
Walking through a field one day, a 17-year-old schoolteacher named George Boole had a vision. His head was full of abstract mathematics — ideas about how to use algebra to solve complex calculus problems. Suddenly, he was struck with a flash of insight: that thought itself might be expressed in algebraic form.
Boole was born on November 2, 1815, at four o’clock in the afternoon, in Lincoln, England. He was the first child of John Boole, a shoemaker, and his wife Mary Ann. But John was no ordinary shoemaker — he was an enthusiast of science and mathematics, as likely to be making telescopes as shoes. Appropriately, his son George received a quality education, studying the classics as well as mathematics and learning to play the flute and piano. He quickly became fluent in Latin and Greek, a…
articles.title: The man who transposed human thought into algebra

articles.author: Ethan Siegel
articles.description: Perhaps the most commonly told myth in all of science is that of the lone genius. The blueprint for it goes something like this. Once upon a time in history, someone with a towering intellect but no formal training wades into a field that’s new to them for the first time. Upon considering the field’s issues, they immediately see things that no one else has ever seen before. With just a little bit of hard work, they find solutions to puzzles that have stymied all of the greatest minds in the field that approached those problems previously. They wind up revolutionizing their field, and the world is never the same. It leaves one with a strong take-home message: that if you were that inexperienced person with a similarly towering intellect, and you had the good fortune of coming into a field j…
articles.title: Einstein the “lone genius” is a complete myth

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: These maple roasted carrots really take advantage of the whole vegetable. Simply seasoned and roasted to tender, caramelized perfection, the carrots are topped with a vibrant, garlicky chimichurri made from the carrot greens themselves. The combo of earthy, subtly sweet carrots next to the bold, tangy sauce is a ten out of ten.
articles.title: Maple Glazed Roasted Carrots with Carrot Greens Chimichurri

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Meet the newest member of your go-to side dish rotation. This vegan cauliflower mash hits the sweet spot between fabulously low-carb and creamy richness. It's made with roasted cauliflower and garlic for the best savoury, caramelized flavour and coconut milk and vegan butter for an ultra-silky, smooth finish. It's perfect for Thanksgiving dinner or really whenever you want it.
articles.title: Vegan Mashed Cauliflower

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Got a few minutes? Make these cinnamon baked pears. Perfectly caramelized in a glossy sauce of maple syrup, cinnamon, and their own sweet juices, these warm, fork-tender pears are everything. Top 'em with coconut cream and crunchy granola, and tell me you haven't found your new favourite fall dessert.
articles.title: Cinnamon Baked Pears

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Three bean salad may have a bit of an old-school reputation, but this one deserves a comeback. Made with creamy kidney beans, hearty chickpeas, and tender blanched green beans, all marinated in a perfectly balanced maple-Dijon dressing, it's tangy, sweet, and about to become your new favourite way to dress up those canned beans.
articles.title: Classic Three Bean Salad

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: This sweet and savoury roasted sweet potato soup is silky smooth and packed with the deeply satisfying flavours of beautifully caramelized oven-roasted veggies, thyme, and warming spices. It's perfect for fall, and all you need is a sheet pan and a blender. You've gotta love it when simple and easy really pays off.
articles.title: Roasted Sweet Potato Soup (Easy Sheet Pan Soup!)

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Looking for new ways to get excited about rice? This easy yellow rice is for you. Cooked in veggie broth and infused with peppery turmeric and warming cumin, it's toasted and simmered to fluffy perfection. Serve it with falafel and homemade hummus for one seriously flavourful Middle Eastern-inspired meal.
articles.title: Yellow Rice

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: As we enter the fall months, cozy apple-y treats are in, and these bakery-style apple cinnamon rolls deserve a place on the menu. Thanks to a few tricks of the trade, they come out so fluffy (almost cloud-like), and the filling tastes like your favourite apple pie. Topped with thick, tangy vegan cream cheese frosting, there's simply nothing like them.
articles.title: Apple Cinnamon Rolls

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Fall is in the air, and if you're still craving those crisp salad greens but starting to get excited about maple syrup and the smell of roasting root veggies, this sweet potato salad recipe is for you. A bed of fresh, peppery arugula is topped with tender, warm roasted sweet potatoes and buttery pecans in a bright, lemony dressing. The perfect transition from summer to fall.
articles.title: Sweet Potato Arugula Salad

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Sometimes you just need a cheesesteak. Right? In those times, this vegan Philly cheesesteak recipe hits the spot. From the golden-brown, chewy, savoury soy curl "steak" bites to the tender sautéed veggies and melted provolone, these sandwiches are filled to the brim with all the fixin's.
articles.title: Soy Curl Philly Cheesesteak

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Have you ever had a fresh tortilla, still steaming from the skillet, covered in golden-brown blisters? There's nothing quite like it. These vegan flour tortillas are soft and tender with the perfect chew. Fold ’em into tacos, turn ’em into quesadillas, or enjoy as is, piping hot, straight out of the pan.
articles.title: Simple Flour Tortillas

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: When life gives you limes, make cilantro lime marinated tofu. Bursting with flavours of bright, zippy lime, fresh, citrusy cilantro, and a hit of garlic, this easy, air fryer tofu comes out perfectly crispy and golden brown with a satisfying chew. Served over rice with an extra drizzle of marinade, dinner never tasted so good.
articles.title: Cilantro Lime Marinated Tofu

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Whether it's game day or dinner time with the kiddos, this vegan popcorn chicken is a winner. Tender, juicy soy curls are wrapped in a crunchy KFC-style breading that'll beat takeout any day. Serve them with creamy maple Dijon sauce and watch them disappear.
articles.title: Vegan Popcorn Chicken

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Not quite ready to bake another loaf, but wondering what to do with that sourdough discard? These easy sourdough discard crackers are the answer. Crunchy, crispy, and flaky with that perfect sourdough tang (and a hint of rosemary), they're ideal for dipping and snacking!
articles.title: Sourdough Discard Crackers

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Italian food lovers, this one's for you. This 5-ingredient vegan baked ziti, with its al dente noodles, savoury marinara sauce, and gooey, melty vegan cheese, married together mouthful after mouthful, is comfort food at its finest. Pop it in the oven in just 20 minutes and watch it bubble up into a new family favourite.
articles.title: Cheesy Baked Ziti

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: These vegan sourdough chocolate chip cookies are so popular in my household that we always have a bag of these frozen cookie dough balls in the freezer. They are the most tender, chewy cookies with a subtle sourdough tang that'll have everyone asking, "What's the secret ingredient?" Dipped in a cool glass of plant-based milk, they are 100% about to change your cookie game forever.
articles.title: Sourdough Discard Chocolate Chip Cookies

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: This easy ratatouille recipe is one of the best ways to enjoy summer's finest veggies. Baked layers of tender eggplant, squash, and tomato brushed with a delicate herb oil sit atop a rich, tangy tomato sauce, just like the French do it. Sounds pretty dreamy, right? Head to the farmers market and get started!
articles.title: Easy Ratatouille Recipe

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: This apple butter needs to be the first on your fall to-make list! Smooth and glossy, it's overflowing with the cozy, warming spices you associate with the season. Cinnamon, nutmeg, cloves, and a hint of vanilla turn sweet 'n tart apples into a spread you'll want to slather on everything in sight.
articles.title: Apple Butter Recipe

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: This blueberry cobbler takes the cake when it comes to blueberry-lisciuous summer desserts. A tender, golden-brown topping sits over this magical blueberry filling that bakes away in the oven into bubbly, gooey, just-sweet-enough heaven. Make it with fresh berries or frozen ones in the off-season.
articles.title: Vegan Blueberry Cobbler

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Rich marinara sauce, melty vegan mozzarella, and protein-packed lentils all stuffed into juicy, tender zucchini boats? Yes please! This Italian-inspired side (or entrée) is easy enough to make on a Monday night and impressive enough to bring to your next snazzy event.
articles.title: Stuffed Zucchini Boats

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Spanish gazpacho is arguably one of the better ways to use those farmers' market tomatoes. Blend 'em with some olive oil, a splash of red wine vinegar, and a few other seasonal veggies, and you've got yourself one of the most refreshing soups in existence. Served chilled with a hunk of crusty bread, it's summer in a bowl.
articles.title: Gazpacho

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: This 25-minute vegan cottage cheese pancake recipe is about to become your go-to, protein-packed breakfast. They're so easy to make and come out perfectly light and fluffy. Grab the maple syrup and get started!
articles.title: Cottage Cheese Pancakes

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: This recipe for vegan cottage cheese couldn't be easier. Perfectly tender tofu "curds" sit in a savoury, tangy, salty sauce and take on an incredibly realistic cottage cheese flavour. You'll see!
articles.title: Vegan Cottage Cheese

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: If you're interested in getting into Jamaican cuisine, this steamed cabbage is a great place to start. This island classic uses simple cooking methods and a few thoughtfully chosen spices to transform simple cabbage into a sweet, savoury, slightly spicy, and totally crave-worthy accompaniment to any Jamaican main.
articles.title: Jamaican Steamed Cabbage

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: This shredded tofu needs to be on your meal prep list. Tossed in a savoury sauce and baked to crispy golden brown, it's the perfect protein addition to any rice or noodle dish, salad, or taco. Enjoy!
articles.title: Shredded Tofu

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: This cheesy vegan smashed broccoli is the perfect way to mix up your veggie routine. Tender on the inside, with the perfect crisp around the edges, it's served with a creamy, garlicky sauce that's sure to impress.
articles.title: Smashed Broccoli

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: This easy vegan yellow cake recipe deserves a place in your baking rotation! Get ready to dive into two layers of moist, tender, golden-yellow cake filled and frosted with silky-smooth chocolate buttercream.
articles.title: Vegan Yellow Cake

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Sweet, savoury, and the perfect amount of spicy, this smooth, chunky mango chutney marries traditional Jamaican and Indian flavours beautifully. It's bursting with warming spices and juicy fruit you'll crave again and again.
articles.title: Mango Chutney

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Taco night just got an upgrade! These vegan soy curl tacos pair perfectly crispy soy curl "chicken" with creamy avocado and crunchy veggies. The icing on the cake? A tangy, creamy lime sauce that's good enough to eat straight out of the bowl. Go ahead, try it!
articles.title: Soy Curl Tacos

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: This vegan chickpea omelette will have the whole fam jumping out of bed and running to the kitchen. Chickpea flour and water come together to make the perfect, tender omelette you can fill with your favourite veggies, vegan cheese, and really anything you'd like. Good morning!
articles.title: Vegan Chickpea Flour Omelette

articles.author: Jessica Hylton
articles.description: Looking for the perfect slice to build your PB&J or avocado toast on? This whole grain sandwich bread is for you. Soft, tender, and surprisingly easy to make, it sure beats the store-bought stuff!
articles.title: Whole Grain Sandwich Bread

articles.description:
This is a story of an old toy webpage that used to entertain kids with hand-drawn animated doodles.
Disclaimer: I’m not a computer vision expert, so many of the mistakes might be obvious to the reader, but nevertheless are part of my story.
I vaguely remember that in the early days of smartphones there was an app that allowed you to print a grid of squares. Then you scribbled some hand-drawn animated frames in each cell.
articles.title: Bunnymator, or impractical computer vision

articles.author: Patrick Coyne
articles.description:
As Election Day approaches, political mudslinging has taken an ugly, slanderous, and, in some ways, literal turn.
 It seems my opponent has decided to ramp up his personal insults by claiming I am not an authentic, down-to-earth politician who only wants to improve his community. He alleges that I am the mud monster from the movie Mulholland Drive.
 A truly preposterous and desperate ploy cooked up by a flailing campaign!
 Initially, I chose not to get mired in the muck and instead focused on my message of affordability. But after consulting with my advisors, I have decided to address this egregious lie directly.
 No, I am not the “mud monster.” That is a fictional character, also referred to as the “dumpster hobo.” Which, I guess if I had to choose between the two, I would much rather be …
articles.title: My Political Opponent Is Lying About Me Being the Mud Monster from Mulholland Drive

articles.author: Ali Fitzgerald
articles.description:
Underground Artists is an ongoing comic by Ali Fitzgerald (Hungover Bear & Friends) that follows woodland creatures as they create art and search out whimsy in a bleak forest.
 - - -
articles.title: Ursine Performance

articles.author: Nathan Cowley
articles.description:
Honestly, I’m fine.
 It’s really not as bad as it looks. The bridge was just a lot lower than expected.
 I appreciate you stopping to help, and hopefully you understand ASL, but you’re fussing over nothing. It’s just a scratch. This kind of thing happens all the time. I’m sure my head will turn up eventually.
 Please, there’s no need to get the hospital involved. The doctors have enough on their plates without having to examine my neck hole. I have a couple of gauze pads in my kitchen cupboard. They should do the trick. Besides, it’s already starting to feel a lot better. I’m almost wondering whether I even need the head at all.
 Plus, Tarrytown General is like half an hour away. It’s a long trip to make for the paramedics. I’m sure they’re sick of people calling ambulances for the smalles…
articles.title: The Headless Horseman Doesn’t Want to Bother the ER

articles.author: Eli Grober
articles.description:
“Anybody reporting Voter Fraud in the past Elections, or the upcoming 2026 Midterm Election, will be paid $1,000,000 upon the arrest and conviction of those that created the Fraud! Thank you for your attention to this matter.” — President Donald Trump
 - - -
There is a scourge on our democracy. A dark cloud that casts a shadow over our electoral system. It calls into question everything we stand for as a nation. For far too long, our elections have been influenced by a cabal of insurgents known as “voters.” Each year they arrive at polling places across the United States to do the unspeakable: fill in ballots. They seem to have infiltrated every facet of our representative system.
 We can’t keep letting the people of this country get away with interfering in the democratic process by parti…
articles.title: We Must Protect Our Elections from Voters

articles.author: Natasha Dumas
articles.description:
ARISTIDES: Greetings, Pheidippides! Why are you covered in sweat?
 PHEIDIPPIDES: It is because I ran all the way here from Marathon. My friend, I bring important news.
 ARISTIDES: Oh, my prayers have been answered! We have all been waiting anxiously for updates. What has happened?
 PHEIDIPPIDES: I have achieved a PR!
 ARISTIDES: A “PR”?
 PHEIDIPPIDES: Oh, I apologize. I forgot you are not a runner. Or rather, you are not yet a runner. PR stands for “Personal Record.” I ran that distance in three hours and thirty minutes. I mean, it is technically the first of its kind, so it would have been a record whatever I did, but I certainly beat my expectations.
 ARISTIDES: What happened with the Persians?
 PHEIDIPPIDES: Hold on one moment. Let me take some time to transcribe the details.
 ARISTIDES…
articles.title: If the First Marathon  Had Been Completed  by a Running Bro

articles.author: Alan Johnson
articles.description:
Hello, neighbors. My name is Grant Sharma, and I’m a managing partner at Haverford Ridge Capital. As of last Tuesday, we are the proud new owners of 2218 Linden Avenue, or, as many of you know it, the House That Gives Out Full-Size Candy Bars.
 First off, nothing is changing.
 Barb built something special here. For thirty-one years, she turned on her porch light, filled a mixing bowl with full-size Snickers and Crunch bars, and sat on the steps in a witch hat saying, “Take two, sweetie.” Kids beg their parents to drive in from other zip codes for this house. You can’t buy that. Well, you can, if you offer 40 percent above asking.
 We are simply here to help it scale. You may notice a few updates.
 Finding the full-size candy bar house is one of childhood’s great moments. We would never tak…
articles.title: I Am the Manager of the Private Equity Firm That Just Acquired the House in Your Neighborhood That Hands Out Full-Size Candy Bars on Halloween

articles.author: Anthony DeThomas
articles.description:
A: Hey, I just saw all the Halloween decorations you put up in the front yard.
 B: Pretty cool, huh?
 A: No. It’s not pretty cool. Why did you get only child-sized skeletons? And why so many of them?
 B: I thought our decorations should tell a story this year.
 A: Okay, well now our house looks like a really sad orphanage.
 B: That’s exactly what I was going for.
 A: Yeah, but what’s with the buckets and brooms?
 B: I thought it would be good for them to learn some discipline with weekly chores.
 A: So the decorations are doing chores?
 B: No, the children are doing chores.
 A: Did you have to put actual children’s shoes on them?
 B: Yes. Mr. Pomerance just donated all of those shoes. It’s the first time most of those children have gotten new shoes. He said, “Every child deserves dignity,”…
articles.title: I Think You Decorated for Halloween Wrong

articles.author: Evan Dotas
articles.description:
“U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche defended his department’s lawsuit seeking to stop Alaska from automatically certifying the results of its Senate election if the Republican incumbent loses… The Justice Department claims that potential confusion over candidates with similar names is the reason for the suit, though some Democrats have argued that it is actually an attempt to interfere in the democratic process.” — NPR
 “I’m the president. I can call him whatever the hell I want. To me, he’s Mohammed, and he’s a radical jihadist.” — President Donald Trump speaking about Michigan Democratic Senatorial Candidate Abdul El-Sayed during a campaign rally.
 - - -
People don’t like to admit it, but voting is hard. Not because rural Americans can’t reliably mail in their ballots or because paramili…
articles.title: How Will People Know Who to Vote for with Two Dan Sullivans and Zero Mohammeds?

articles.author: Chason Gordon
articles.description:
I know you see me running backwards on the treadmill while doing lunges at seventeen-second intervals. What do you do? Just jog on it facing forward? Amateur.
 Using a gym machine the way it’s meant to be used is for losers. Why even show up unless you’re going to damage equipment and move your body in a multidimensional way no one’s ever seen before?
 I do a constant wheelie on the exercise bike, walk down the stairs on the Stairmaster, and use the elliptical like it’s a 360-degree gyroscope NASA trains astronauts with. The machines often stop working after I’m done, but that’s not my problem.
 Most people just come here and do their basic reps. I work the equipment so hard that many of them naturally become airborne. If you’re using the recumbent bike and it doesn’t begin hovering three …
articles.title: I’m the Guy Who Uses Gym Equipment in Ways You’ve Never Seen

articles.author: Julie Klausner
articles.description:
1. Wait, for real?
 2. When is Halloween anyway?

articles.author: Devin Wallace
articles.description:
If you’re so tired of expensive housing prices in your major city, then why don’t you stop complaining and move to this random town I found with some cheap houses for sale and exactly zero other amenities?
 No place is perfect. Sure, this city is in the middle of nowhere, isn’t near major job markets, and doesn’t have maintained roads, well-funded schools, or functioning emergency services, but it does have a series of dilapidated ranch houses located between a data center and a second data center that is currently on fire.
 You can’t complain about the price of housing if you refuse to move hundreds of miles away to a city I just learned about for the purposes of this bad-faith argument.
 For the same amount as a down payment in New York City, you could buy an entire house in this town in upstate wherever or whatever it’s called. You could also buy absolutely nothing else in the town because any industry was decimated in a post-industrial economic order that bled regional metros dry for the benefit of a handful of global conglomerates.
 So… should I rent the U-Haul?
 With the money you’ll save on housing, you can afford dozens of flights and train trips across the country to see the aging relatives, friends, and entire community of people you’ve abandoned.
 You’ll never worry about a ludicrously high rent payment again. Instead, you can worry about your new neighbors, most of whom have been left behind by violent austerity measures strangling the last drops of life out of previously vibrant towns and cities.
 I did this exact thing when I was young. I packed my bags, left my major city, and moved all the way to a redlined suburb fifteen minutes outside that city, built specifically for people who looked like me. If I can do that, young people should be willing to live on an active Superfund site covered in broken glass.
 I think moving there is something thousands of young people should consider, and no, I will not consider what would happen to housing costs if thousands of young people moved there.
articles.title: Why Aren’t People Moving to This Town with Cheap Housing and Literally Nothing Else?

Grandma, it’s the first of the month. Did you forget the blood tithe was due? Don’t worry, Gam-Gam, I’ll help you figure it out.
 You can’t pay for anything by card anymore. That stopped being a thing in the 2030s. The Data Lord doesn’t take AmEx. It’s half a pint now, or a full pint every two months, and you’re on a monthly plan. Hold your arm out, and I’ll get the tourniquet. There we go.
 I know, times have changed a lot, huh? Back in your day, people used money for this kind of thing. But the Data Lord has all the money, so now we just pay with blood instead. It’s even easier, if you think about it. No need to worry about “savings” or “inflation” or whatever it is your generation was so obsessed with. Now it’s all about platelet count.
 Oh, don’t be morbid. Of course he doesn’t drink i…
articles.title: It’s Cute How Grandma Doesn’t Even Know How to Blood Tithe to the Data Lord

articles.author: Taylor Harris
articles.description:
You’ve Always Been This Way is a column written by Taylor Harris, a late-diagnosed neurodivergent woman and 1980s preschool dropout, who identifies every moment from her past that filled her with shame, and mutters, “Yep, that tracks. I see it all now.”
 - - -
Toni Morrison famously said, “If there’s a book you want to read, but it hasn’t been written yet, then you must write it.” Well, I wrote the book. And now, for the lady, perhaps a writing endeavor that does not cost three-fourths of her soul? Enter: A free online quiz—the first of its kind—to tell you if your neuros are normal or if they diverge.
 It’s simple. Just circle every answer that resonates with you, and count the number you circled, out of sixty, at the end.
 I’ve done the hard work for you, sifting through every memory and…
articles.title: Is it AuDHD…  or Are You Just Strange?  A Seventeen Magazine–Style Quiz for Millennials

articles.author: Luís Leal Miranda
articles.description:
He steals from the rich to give to the poor, which sounds generous until you learn what he steals.
 The people of Sherwood do not need six unmatched salt shakers, twenty-three hotel towels, or a bag of decorative seashells.
 And yet, every few days, Robin bursts into the village grinning like a man who just dug up a treasure.
 “Good news!” he announces, carefully setting down a ceramic owl. “She’s heavy, so she must be worth something.”
 “We are starving, Robin,” the villagers reply.
 Robin nods sympathetically before handing an orphan three decorative soaps and a laminated loyalty card for a frozen yogurt chain that no longer exists.
 During one raid on Prince John’s castle, while the others searched for gold, Robin filled two sacks with teaspoons from the royal cafeteria and a framed pho…
articles.title: Robin Hood, Prince of Compulsive and Pointless Theft

articles.author: John Howard Matthews
articles.description:
Dear Astral Skye Data Center Workers,
 When A-Skye first took possession of four thousand acres of your town’s land to build an AI facility the size of three thousand football fields, it gave some of you pause.
 You wanted transparency. You wanted oversight. While we couldn’t provide either of those things, we more than made up for it in deceit and unkept promises.
 When we opened, we needed just a smidge more water than anticipated, and your wells dried up.
 When your electric bills skyrocketed, it was our bad.
 In the space of a year, we destroyed the tight-knit fabric that held this community of 130 citizens together. That’s also on us.
 Another thing we didn’t anticipate was not being able to provide three hundred good-paying jobs that didn’t require special training or college degrees…
articles.title: Announcing Our AI Data Center’s First Take Your Child to Work Day

articles.author: Nathaniel Missildine
articles.description:
Steer Clear
 When spotting another American in a foreign country, your first instinct is usually the correct one: run in the opposite direction. Like you, this person has come here to blot out, even if for a bewildered weekend, the very idea of the place they left behind. The last thing either one of you needs right now is the reminder of how lost you are, both in an unprecedented, historic sense, and also in the center of this lovely, cobblestoned town.
 If Unavoidable, Approach with Caution
 At the same time, there’s not much point in attempting the mutual charade that you two haven’t noticed one another. Nor is there any reason to pretend that wearing a scarf and a collared shirt with the sleeves jauntily rolled up means you pass as a local. So, approach your fellow American at the icon…
articles.title: Travel Tips When Encountering Fellow Americans Abroad

articles.author: Paige Collings
articles.description:
In today’s digital world, the internet is an essential resource for young people to access information, explore community, and find themselves. But we know that this often comes alongside fears of experiencing online harms like doxxing, grooming, or bullying.
Trying to protect your family from everything all the time is impractical and exhausting, but some thoughtful planning can help families devise a workable plan that meets their needs and addresses their concerns.
That’s why this Digital Parent Week, we’re sharing easy tips on how parents and their children can work together to co-curate a digital safety plan that helps all members of the family enjoy the benefits of technology while protecting their online privacy and safety. 
Start with Open Conversations
Online safety begins with co…

In the most recent update to Apple’s devices, iOS 27.2, the company has introduced a new setting to “Exclude Apps” from Siri AI, fulfilling one of our asks from our Encrypt It Already campaign earlier this year.
One of our main concerns with new AI features on devices is how those features interact with end-to-end encrypted content, particularly with secure messaging apps. Many AI features require cloud processing, and despite privacy protections engineered into these systems, the content of secure messaging apps may leave a user’s device without their knowledge. That changes the privacy concerns around using those tools. In a perfect world, users would be able to put a barrier up to ensure data from certain apps doesn’t leave the device. Here was our initial ask:

articles.author: Mario Trujillo
articles.description:
A federal appeals court should curb the government’s abuse of grand jury subpoenas to unmask social media users who criticize lawless immigration enforcement.
That is the message from the ACLU, EFF, and other civil liberties and trade groups who filed a friend-of-the-court brief in a sealed case in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia.
The case involves the government’s investigation of an anonymous Reddit user who commented on a post about an immigration officer in Minnesota. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) first issued an administrative subpoena to Reddit to unmask the user. When the user challenged the subpoena in court on free speech and statutory grounds (as many others have), DHS withdrew it. But then the government obtained a separate grand jury subpoena—…

But in a betrayal of that trust, the federal government has been pooling the information it has about us on an unprecedented scale—and using it for purposes we never agreed to.

articles.description:
A nonprofit service that protects internet users’ privacy is leaving France. Quad9, a free DNS resolver, has said it will reluctantly stop serving users in France on November 24. This follows a French court order that Quad9 must block access to websites that are accused of infringing the copyrights of a sports broadcaster. Forcing a responsible privacy service out of an important market is a predictable result of trying to force infrastructure providers to be copyright police.
When you visit a website, a DNS resolver reads the domain name you type in—like eff.org— and translates it into a numerical IP address that’s used to direct data across the internet. A DNS resolver can see the names of websites you connect to, so its privacy policies are important. Quad9 is an NGO that’s incorporated…

Any piece of software that anyone actually uses will have a security vulnerability somewhere in the code. The more complex that software is, the more likely there will be a vulnerability. Until recently there was a steady background hum of vulnerabilities being found and patched, with major vulnerabilities that could cripple the entire internet only happening every few years. Automated license plate readers (ALPRs) are mass surveillance. They photograph every passing car and log where and when it was captured, building a searchable record of where nearly everyone drives. Cities should not buy them, and cities that already have them should shut them down.

A warrant requirement would not make mass surveillance acceptable, but it would require police to justify a search to a judge before accessing records of people’s movements. articles.author: Josh Richman
articles.description:
Barry Steinhardt, a lifelong privacy champion and an early leader in the battle for digital civil liberties who served as EFF’s president in 1998-99, died last week at age 73. 
A Connecticut native, Steinhardt led the Vermont and Pennsylvania affiliates of the American Civil Liberties Union before becoming associate director of the national ACLU. There, he helped spearhead the fight to overturn much of the Communications Decency Act, resulting in the U.S. Supreme Court’s landmark Reno v. ACLU ruling in 1997. 
When the internet was still young, Steinhardt became one of the first attorneys to specialize in the intersection of technology and privacy. In early 1998 he took a leave of absence from the ACLU to become EFF’s president, and then returned to the ACLU in 1999. 
In 2002 he founded the ACLU’s Program on Technology and Liberty. After retiring from the ACLU, he continued on as a senior advisor to London-based Privacy International. 
Steinhardt chaired the 2003 Computer Freedom and Privacy Conference and served on a wide variety of significant panels and boards, including the Department of Transportation’s Negotiated Rule Making on national driver’s license standards, the Advisory Committee to the US Census, and the Blue Ribbon Panel on Genetics of the National Conference of State Legislatures. He also was selected to be a member of the US delegation to the G-8 Government and Private Sector Tokyo conference on Cyber Crime and served as an advisor to the Czech Helsinki Committee.  
“Barry led many critical technology and civil liberties fights and was an important mentor to me and others in the field,” said EFF Executive Director Nicole Ozer. “Barry’s influential work across strategy to defend and advance privacy rights and safeguard people against surveillance has made its mark on the law and policy of our digital world and protected the rights and safety of people across the United States and around the world.”
articles.title: In Memoriam: Barry Steinhardt

Over the years, the major tech companies have found all sorts of ways to embed themselves into our lives. We often use their software, their AI tools, their social media, and their operating systems by default without even thinking about potential alternatives. It’s time to rethink that relationship. 
Last year, we created Opt Out October to help remind ourselves of the variety of ways we can take back control of our data through small steps inside apps, operating systems, and other various forms. This year, we highlight the idea that sometimes the best way to control your data is to leave a platform, app, or operating system altogether. 
To do so, we’ve created a hub of resources sharing ways to find new software that isn’t made by the tech giants, take advantage of the growing universe of new social media options, install a whole new operating system, and better control how various popular tools and software use your data for AI training. 
As an incentive, we’ve made merit badges like the one below to help you track your own wins and share them with others. Complete any of these tasks and let the world know by sharing that accomplishment on social media or changing your profile image! Better, more privacy-respecting, and less-enshittified tools are out there. We just have to find and use them.

Head over to our Opt Out October landing page and start taking the first steps to regaining control of the tools and software you use.

The term “digital sovereignty” has become ubiquitous. European officials invoke it in debates about cloud infrastructure, AI, semiconductors, and platform regulation. But digital sovereignty could be something more: an opportunity for users around the world to build more resilient, open  systems and the skills and infrastructure to maintain them.

articles.description:
The Senate Commerce Committee will vote this week on several censorious and privacy invasive bills: KOSA, the SCREEN Act, Youth AI Privacy Act, and CHATBOT Act. While we appreciate that the Committee is taking the time to look at these bills separately, it’s still impossible to ignore the message Congress is sending to the world: Age-gate the internet and block young people from speaking and accessing lawful speech online. Or else. 
Take action
Tell Congress: don't age-gate the internet
Each of these bills claims to be trying to protect children and teenagers from dangerous situations on and offline—certainly a worthy goal. But the proposed solutions in these bills are unlikely to make children and teenagers safer at all. Rather, they would create sweeping new privacy and data security problems, and force platforms to adopt unconstitutional restrictions on the content they host, for both adults and teenagers. 
There is a better way. Instead of considering these bills, the Senate Commerce Committee should be focusing on a national consumer privacy bill that would protect ALL internet users, or on banning behavioral advertising that tracks us across the web—again, for users of all ages. 
But the bills being considered this week move in the other direction—more information being collected, more surveillance, and less privacy for internet users of all ages. 
Take action
help eff oppose these bills
EFF sent a letter to the Committee with our concerns about these bills. We look forward to continuing to work with them to find a way forward that protects all users.
articles.title: Tomorrow’s U.S. Senate Vote: Four Internet Bills, One Wrong Direction
